unit_label: Module A: International Banking - Exports and Imports of goods and services

facts.statement: Export of goods or software may be made without the declaration form in these cases: trade samples and publicity material supplied free of payment; personal effects of travellers; ship's stores, trans-shipment cargo and goods supplied under Government or defence orders; tugs, dredgers and offshore support vessels subject to re-import; gifts of goods with an exporter's declaration that the value is not more than five lakh rupees; aircraft and engines sent for overhaul or repair abroad and re-imported within six months; goods imported free of cost on a re-export basis; defective or loaned or surplus imported goods that a Development Commissioner permits to be re-exported from a special economic zone, technology park or free trade zone; replacement goods exported free under the Foreign Trade Policy; goods sent out for testing subject to re-import; defective goods sent for repair and re-import with an authorised dealer's certificate that no foreign exchange is involved; and exports the Reserve Bank permits on application. An exemption from the declaration does not remove the duty to realise and repatriate export proceeds.
facts.locator: Regulation 4(a) to (k); Master Direction on Export of Goods and Services, paragraph B.12

facts.statement: An authorised dealer may grant a waiver of the declaration form (EDF) for status holder exporters sending freely exportable goods free of cost for export promotion, up to an annual limit of two per cent of the average annual export realisation of the preceding three licensing years (excluding gems and jewellery and articles of gold and precious metals); for those excluded sectors the limit is the lower of rupees one crore or two per cent; for supplies of pharmaceutical products, vaccines and lifesaving drugs to international or government health programmes the limit is up to eight per cent. Such free-of-cost supplies earn no duty drawback or other incentive. Exports that involve no foreign exchange transaction, directly or indirectly, need a waiver of the declaration procedure from the Reserve Bank.

Invoicing, payment and settlement of exports and imports in Indian rupees is permitted. Settlement takes place through Special Rupee Vostro Accounts (SRVAs) that authorised dealers open for a bank resident outside India or a branch of an Indian bank abroad. An Indian importer pays in rupees into the partner correspondent bank's SRVA against supplier invoices, and an Indian exporter is paid in rupees from the balance in the SRVA. The account may be funded by inward remittances or by transfers from other repatriable rupee accounts; balances may be invested in debt instruments as the investment directions allow; an additional current account may be opened for settlement of trade transactions; and FEDAI publishes a directory of SRVAs. This is an additional arrangement beside settlement in foreign currency and through the Asian Clearing Union. The Master Direction paragraph on international trade settlement in rupees was substituted on 17 July 2026, after the cut-off date used here.
facts.locator: Paragraph A.3(vii) and the INR settlement paragraph

facts.statement: An authorised dealer may allow set-off of outstanding export receivables against outstanding import payables with the same overseas buyer or supplier, or among overseas group and associate companies through a centralised settlement arrangement, on a net or gross basis, if: one authorised dealer operates and supervises the arrangement; the dealer is satisfied about bona fides and KYC; the invoices are not under investigation; Asian Clearing Union transactions stay outside it; goods are not set off against services; both legs are outstanding and fall in the same calendar year; bilateral set-off rests on a verifiable agreement and group set-off on a written enforceable contract; it does not lead to tax avoidance; each export and import is still reported gross in the monitoring systems using the set-off indicator.

Units in special economic zones may net export receivables against import payments if: the netting is with the same Indian entity and the same overseas buyer or supplier (bilateral) and is done as at the balance sheet date of the unit; the exports are documented on the export declaration form (or DTR) and the imports on the A1 or A2 form, and the export form is treated as complete only after the entire proceeds are adjusted or received; sales and purchases are reported separately in the R-returns; ACU-country transactions stay outside it; all documents go to the authorised dealer.

Authorised dealers update the export monitoring system on an as-and-when-realised basis and generate the electronic bank realisation certificate (eBRC) only from the data in that system, from 16 October 2017. For entries of ₹10 lakh or less per entry or bill, the bank closes and reconciles them on the exporter's declaration that the amount has been realised, and accepts a reduction in declared or invoice value on the exporter's declaration; declarations may be taken quarterly for several bills together. The bank reviews its handling charges for small-value export transactions and does not levy penal charges for delays in adhering to regulatory guidelines.

An exporter receiving an advance payment must ship within three years of receipt, may pay interest of not more than the benchmark rate plus 100 basis points, and must route the shipping documents through the authorised dealer that received the advance; after three years no refund or interest may be remitted without the Reserve Bank's approval. An exporter with at least three years' satisfactory record may receive a long-term advance up to ten years for long-term supply contracts, subject to conditions including firm irrevocable orders and a vetted contract, capacity to execute, clean enforcement record, adjustment through future exports, interest not above the benchmark plus 200 basis points, documents through one dealer, no use to liquidate NPA rupee loans, no double financing, and immediate reporting to the Reserve Bank of an advance of USD 100 million or more.

Authorised dealers and EXIM Bank may undertake forfaiting of export receivables; commitment fees and service charges may be remitted in advance as a lump sum or monthly. Authorised dealers may factor export receivables on a non-recourse basis, at their own business decision: they must not over-finance the client, may size working capital from the invoices purchased, which must be genuine trade invoices; the export factor needs an arrangement with an import factor for credit evaluation and collection, and a notation must be made on the invoice that the importer pays the import factor; after factoring the export factor may close the export bills and report in the export monitoring system; where there is no import factor the export factor may take credit details from the correspondent bank abroad; and KYC and due diligence on the exporter are the export factor's duty.

Advance remittance for imports of goods may be allowed without a ceiling. If the advance exceeds USD 200,000 the bank obtains an unconditional irrevocable standby letter of credit or a guarantee from an international bank of repute outside India (or from an Indian authorised dealer against such a bank's counter-guarantee). For a private importer unable to obtain one, a dealer satisfied about track record may waive it up to USD 5 million, under a Board-approved policy. A public sector company or Government department that cannot obtain a guarantee needs a waiver from the Ministry of Finance for an advance above USD 100,000. Remittances for imports should be completed within six months of shipment; dealers may extend the time for settlement by up to six months at a time, to a maximum of three years, and for an extension beyond one year from the date of remittance the importer's total outstanding must not exceed the lower of USD one million or 10 per cent of the average import remittances of the preceding two financial years.

On every outward advance remittance for imports the authorised dealer creates an Outward Remittance Message (ORM) in the import monitoring system (IDPMS); the bill of entry is downloaded from the BoE master for ports with electronic data interchange, or uploaded by the dealer for other ports; an extension of time is reported as a "Bill of Entry Extension" with the extension date; and the dealer follows the bill of entry evidence through the system.

Trade credit means credit extended by the overseas supplier, bank or financial institution for permissible imports, and includes supplier's credit (extended by the overseas supplier) and buyer's credit (a loan arranged by the importer from an overseas bank or institution to pay for imports). Under the schedule on trade credit importers may raise it for capital and non-capital goods, in foreign currency or rupees, up to USD 50 million per import transaction; for up to one year linked to the operating cycle for non-capital goods and up to three years for capital goods, reckoned from the date of shipment; from overseas suppliers, banks and financial institutions, foreign equity holders and IFSC institutions; with cost not above 250 basis points over the six-month benchmark for foreign currency credit and market-linked cost for rupee credit; with security and guarantees permitted, and authorised dealers may issue guarantees in favour of the overseas lender. Trade credit of original maturity up to three years is not treated as external commercial borrowing; deferred payment arrangements within those periods are treated as trade credit.
facts.locator: Schedule II; Import MD paragraph B.5.2

payload.title: Exports that need no declaration form
payload.core_explanation_md:
The declaration form (EDF) is the exporter's statement to the bank and customs of what is leaving. **Regulation 4** lists cases where **no declaration is needed**:

- **Trade samples** and **publicity material** supplied **free**.
- **Personal effects** of travellers.
- **Ship's stores**, **trans-shipment cargo** and goods supplied to **Government or defence** orders.
- **Gifts** with an exporter's declaration that the value is **not more than ₹5 lakh**.
- **Aircraft and engines** sent abroad for overhaul or repair and **re-imported within six months**.
- Goods **imported free on a re-export basis**; goods sent abroad **for testing** (to be re-imported); **replacement goods** exported free under the Foreign Trade Policy.
- **Defective goods sent for repair and re-import**, with an **authorised dealer's certificate that no foreign exchange is involved**.
- Re-export of **defective, loaned or surplus imported goods** that a **Development Commissioner** (SEZ, technology park, free trade zone) permits.
- Exports **the Reserve Bank permits** on application.

**Important**: no form does **not** mean no obligation: the exporter must still **realise and repatriate** the proceeds.

payload.title: Waiver of the declaration form and the status holder free-of-cost limit
payload.core_explanation_md:
Where **no foreign exchange is involved at all**, the **Reserve Bank** must waive the declaration procedure. An **authorised dealer** may, however, **waive the form** for **status holder** exporters who send **freely exportable goods free of cost** to promote exports, within a yearly cap:

| Exporter | Annual cap on free-of-cost exports |
| --- | --- |
| Most exporters | **2%** of the **average annual export realisation of the last three licensing years** |
| Gems and jewellery; gold and precious metals articles | the **lower of ₹1 crore and 2%** |
| Supplies of **vaccines, drugs, pharmaceuticals** to UN, WHO-PAHO or Government **health programmes** | up to **8%** |

Such free supplies get **no duty drawback or other export incentive**.

payload.title: Trade in rupees: invoicing and settlement through the Special Rupee Vostro Account
payload.core_explanation_md:
Exports and imports may be **invoiced, paid and settled in rupees**, as an **additional** route beside foreign currency and the Asian Clearing Union.

**How the money moves**
- An **authorised dealer in India** opens a **Special Rupee Vostro Account (SRVA)** for a **bank resident outside India** (or a branch of an Indian bank abroad).
- **Importer in India** pays **rupees** into the partner bank's SRVA against the supplier's invoice.
- **Exporter in India** is paid **rupees out of the balance** in the SRVA.
- The SRVA can be funded by **inward remittances** or transfers from other **repatriable rupee accounts**.
- The dealer may open an **additional current account** exclusively for settling trade.
- **FEDAI** publishes a **directory of SRVAs**.

**Limit of this card**: the Master Direction's own paragraph on rupee trade settlement was **rewritten on 17 July 2026**, after the cut-off date used for this course. The account mechanics above are the stable part.

payload.title: Set-off and netting of export receivables against import payables
Advance received for exports: three years, interest cap and long-term advances
eBRC and closing small export entries by declaration
payload.core_explanation_md:
The **export monitoring system (EDPMS)** records each export and its realisation.

- Banks update it **as and when proceeds are realised**.
- The **electronic bank realisation certificate (eBRC)** is generated **only from EDPMS data** (since **16 October 2017**), so the two always agree.

**Small entries: ₹10 lakh or less per entry or bill**
- The bank **reconciles and closes** them on the **exporter's declaration** that the money has been realised.
- A **reduction in declared or invoice value** is also accepted on the exporter's declaration.
- Declarations may be taken **quarterly**, covering **several bills together**.
- The bank **reviews its charges** on such small transactions and levies **no penalty** for delay in following regulatory guidelines.

Above ₹10 lakh the usual proof of realisation applies.

payload.title: Forfaiting and non-recourse export factoring
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Forfaiting**: **EXIM Bank and authorised dealers** may **buy export receivables without recourse to the exporter**; commitment fees and service charges may be paid **in advance as a lump sum or monthly**.

**Export factoring on a non-recourse basis**
- A bank decides **for itself** whether to factor; it must **not over-finance** the client and the invoices must be **genuine trade invoices**.
- The **export factor** needs an arrangement with an **import factor** abroad for **credit evaluation and collection**.
- The invoice carries a **notation that the importer pays the import factor**.
- After factoring, the export factor may **close the export bills** and report in **EDPMS**.
- With **no import factor**, the export factor may take credit information from the **correspondent bank abroad**.
- The export factor does **KYC and due diligence on the exporter**.

payload.title: Advance remittance for imports and the time to settle import dues
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Advance remittance for goods**: no ceiling, but:

| Advance | What the bank needs |
| --- | --- |
| **Up to USD 200,000** | no guarantee |
| **Above USD 200,000** | an **unconditional irrevocable standby L/C or guarantee** from an **international bank of repute** (or an Indian AD's guarantee against that bank's counter-guarantee) |
| Private importer **unable to get a guarantee** | dealer may waive up to **USD 5 million**, if satisfied on **track record**, under a **Board-approved policy** |
| **PSU/Government** unable to get one | **Ministry of Finance waiver** for an advance **above USD 100,000** |

**Time limits**: remit import payments within **six months** of shipment. A dealer may **extend by six months at a time, up to three years**; to go **beyond one year from the date of remittance**, the importer's **total outstanding** must be within the **lower of USD 1 million and 10% of the average import remittances of the previous two financial years**.

payload.title: IDPMS: the outward remittance message and the bill of entry
payload.core_explanation_md:
The **import monitoring system (IDPMS)** matches **money out** with **goods in**.

- On each **advance remittance** the bank creates an **Outward Remittance Message (ORM)**.
- The **bill of entry**: for **electronic ports** the bank **downloads it from the BoE master** using the importer's AD code; for other ports the bank **uploads** the data.
- The bill of entry is then **marked against the ORM**, closing the loop.
- An **extension of time** is reported as a **"Bill of Entry Extension"**, with the **extension date** entered.

If goods have not come in, the bank follows up and, where the supplier fails to deliver, the advance must be **brought back**.

payload.title: Trade credit: supplier's credit, buyer's credit and the ceilings
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Trade credit** = credit from an **overseas supplier, bank or institution** to pay for **permissible imports**.

- **Supplier's credit**: given by the **overseas supplier**.
- **Buyer's credit**: a **loan the importer arranges from an overseas bank** to pay the supplier.

| Feature | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Amount | up to **USD 50 million per import transaction** |
| Period (from **date of shipment**) | **non-capital goods**: up to **one year** (linked to the operating cycle); **capital goods**: up to **three years** |
| Currency | any **freely convertible currency** or **rupees** |
| Cost (foreign currency) | **not more than 250 bp over the 6-month benchmark** |
| Cost (rupee) | **market-linked** |
| Lenders | overseas suppliers, banks, financial institutions, **foreign equity holders**, **IFSC** institutions |

Trade credit of **original maturity up to three years is not ECB**.

payload.title: The yearly free-of-cost export limit
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a status holder exporter has realised ₹18,00,00,000, ₹24,00,00,000 and ₹30,00,00,000 in the three preceding licensing years. It sells articles of gold (excluded sector). A general merchant exporter with the same figures also wants to send free samples for promotion. Find each limit.

worked_steps.description: 2% of the average, which is the cap for the general exporter.
For the gold articles exporter the cap is the lower of ₹1 crore and 2%.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: General exporter: ₹48,00,000 a year; gold articles exporter: also ₹48,00,000, as 2% is below the ₹1 crore ceiling

payload.title: Extending an import payment beyond one year
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: an importer paid for an import and now asks its bank for further extension beyond one year from the date of remittance. Its import remittances were USD 6,400,000 in one financial year and USD 8,800,000 in the other of the preceding two. Its total outstanding on delayed payments would be USD 900,000. May the bank extend?

Ten per cent of the average.
The ceiling is the lower of USD one million and that figure.
Compare the importer's total outstanding with the ceiling.

payload.stem_md: An importer's import remittances were USD 5,200,000 in one of the two preceding financial years and USD 7,400,000 in the other. Beyond one year from the date of remittance, what is the greatest total outstanding on extended payments the bank can allow, in USD?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Average = (5,200,000 + 7,400,000) ÷ 2 = 6,300,000. Ten per cent = 630,000, which is lower than USD 1,000,000, so the ceiling is 630,000.

worked_solution_steps.description: Lower of USD 1 million and that figure

payload.stem_md: A status holder exporter of garments realised ₹42 crore, ₹45 crore and ₹48 crore in the three preceding licensing years. What is its annual cap on free-of-cost exports, in rupees?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Average = (42 + 45 + 48) crore ÷ 3 = ₹45 crore. Two per cent of ₹45,00,00,000 = ₹90,00,000.
